principles.title: Organize the experience around goals and a coherent user model

source.heading: AF-01 — Organize the experience around goals and a coherent user model

triggers: A new product, navigation structure, or feature that mirrors services, database tables, or an organization chart.
principles.exceptions: The model is a research-informed hypothesis, not a designer's assumption about all people. Technical constraints still exist; present their consequences intelligibly when relevant.

verification.question: Can intended users locate a main task and predict its next action using the exposed objects and vocabulary?

principles.title: Separate user evidence, domain knowledge, and design conjecture

source.heading: AF-02 — Separate user evidence, domain knowledge, and design conjecture

triggers: Discovery, competitor research, a persona, or a claim that a screen solves a user problem.
principles.exceptions: No fixed interview count guarantees understanding. Mobbin evidence describes an interface; AI interpretation does not become participant evidence. Avoid importing the book's stronger criticisms of particular methods as universal exclusions.

verification.question: Can each consequential claim about users be traced to its source and distinguished from the team's interpretation?

principles.title: Use behavioral personas honestly, including provisional ones

source.heading: AF-03 — Use behavioral personas honestly, including provisional ones

triggers: Several audiences, conflicting workflows, or an ambiguous target user.
principles.exceptions: Do not invent quotations, research participants, statistical precision, or demographic stereotypes. Accessibility and rare serious consequences are not disposable because a persona is secondary.

verification.question: Which actual design decision changes because of each evidenced audience trait, and which traits remain assumptions?

principles.title: Define context scenarios and needs before committing to screens

source.heading: AF-04 — Define context scenarios and needs before committing to screens

triggers: Starting a flow, choosing an interaction framework, or jumping directly into polished mockups.
principles.exceptions: The book's aspirational “magic” exercise is an ideation device, not permission to hide consequences or automate actions without intent. A scenario is not a usability test.

verification.question: Can a scenario be traced from its trigger to an outcome with the required information and decisions available at each step?

principles.title: Validate the main path, alternatives, and consequential exceptions

source.heading: AF-05 — Validate the main path, alternatives, and consequential exceptions

triggers: A proposed flow appears complete because its ideal sequence looks convincing.
principles.exceptions: Low frequency is not low importance when harm, exclusion, or loss is high. The book's preference for probable cases must not erase such situations. Expert walkthrough findings remain predictions until tested with users.

verification.question: After backtracking, interruption, cancellation, or a consequential failure, can the task reach a defined completion or recovery state with appropriate work retained?

principles.title: Develop visual direction alongside behavior and emotional intent

source.heading: AF-06 — Develop visual direction alongside behavior and emotional intent

triggers: Selecting a visual style, comparing references, or producing screens that look unrelated across a flow.
principles.exceptions: Attributes are decision criteria, not a substitute for measurable usability or access. A style guide alone does not establish a coherent design language. Do not claim one universally optimal visual or behavioral framework.

verification.question: Across representative states, do visual choices consistently express the stated character while intended users can still identify the task and action?

principles.title: Keep design, implementation, and validation in a continuing conversation

source.heading: AF-07 — Keep design, implementation, and validation in a continuing conversation

triggers: Delegating agents, handing off a design, or discovering feasibility constraints during development.
principles.exceptions: The book discusses human teams; agent roles are this skill's adaptation, not evidence that AI reviewers represent users. It explicitly revises an earlier belief that all design must precede coding.

verification.question: Can each implementation compromise be traced to its effect on a user goal and a check of the affected path?

principles.title: Transfer a pattern's reasoning, not just its appearance

source.heading: AF-08 — Transfer a pattern's reasoning, not just its appearance

triggers: Choosing Mobbin references or reusing a familiar component.
principles.exceptions: Adoption by a polished product is not evidence of success. Historical screenshots, such as the book's drawer examples, are neither current platform requirements nor universal defaults.

verification.question: For each adopted reference, are the observed mechanism, fit, tradeoff, and unverified behaviors explicit?

principles.title: Make assistance considerate, transparent, and recoverable

source.heading: AF-09 — Make assistance considerate, transparent, and recoverable

triggers: Defaults, remembered settings, automation, drafts, sharing, or background work.
principles.exceptions: Do not translate suggestions to remember everything or work proactively into unrestricted collection or action. Incomplete drafts must remain distinguishable from valid committed records. Compute, battery, bandwidth, and privacy constrain assistance.

verification.question: After cancellation, account change, or restart, does assistance retain only appropriate work and accurately show scope, audience, and pending effects?

principles.title: Choose structure for the actual platform and use posture

source.heading: AF-10 — Choose structure for the actual platform and use posture

triggers: Moving a web design to iOS, adding tablet support, or choosing density and navigation.
principles.exceptions: A phone does not guarantee a brief session, nor does desktop imply fullscreen. The book's 2014 device ratios, multitasking limits, and platform predictions are historical.

verification.question: On the intended device and in the actual use context, can people complete the task with workable density, input effort, and interruptions?

principles.title: Support learning and fluency without hiding essential actions

source.heading: AF-11 — Support learning and fluency without hiding essential actions

triggers: A feature serves first-time, occasional, frequent, and expert users.
principles.exceptions: Do not assume every novice becomes expert, impose a fixed click limit, or expose dangerous commands as effortless shortcuts. Progressive disclosure can create search and navigation costs.

verification.question: Can first-time and returning users find the essential route, and can practiced users complete frequent work efficiently without losing its meaning?

principles.title: Remove unnecessary work while preserving orientation

source.heading: AF-12 — Remove unnecessary work while preserving orientation

triggers: A flow has repeated detours, reentry, unclear location, or a deceptively minimal screen.
principles.exceptions: Not all navigation, hierarchy, confirmation, or scrolling is waste. Deliberate steps may support understanding or consequential decisions. Reject universal pane counts and mechanically copied physical limitations.

verification.question: Which context switches, remembered facts, or repeated entries can be removed while preserving a person's understanding of the decision?

principles.title: Make manipulation discoverable and its effects perceivable

source.heading: AF-13 — Make manipulation discoverable and its effects perceivable

triggers: Gestures, custom controls, drag-and-drop, hidden actions, or a novel visual metaphor.
principles.exceptions: Direct manipulation is not always easiest. Do not assume one exposure guarantees learning or force every interaction into a physical metaphor. Tutorials cannot compensate for all hidden controls; current platform conventions govern long press and gestures.

verification.question: Can a first-time user discover the manipulation, perceive its effect, cancel it, and complete the same task through an accessible alternative?

principles.title: Accept meaningful input without silently changing intent

source.heading: AF-14 — Accept meaningful input without silently changing intent

triggers: Forms, structured fields, numerical settings, or incomplete records.
principles.exceptions: Flexibility never removes necessary security or data-integrity checks. Do not silently clamp material values, guess addresses, replace user meaning, or apply the book's fixed validation timing to every field.

verification.question: Do paste, partial input, locale variants, and unusual valid values preserve meaning and remain correctable after validation fails?

principles.title: Make persistence, copies, and versions match the user's intention

source.heading: AF-15 — Make persistence, copies, and versions match the user's intention

triggers: Editing, autosave, document creation, export, or collaborative work.
principles.exceptions: Autosave is not publication or consent to send; local persistence is not confirmed remote synchronization. Versioning must respect privacy, retention, collaboration, and backend constraints. Do not promise unlimited history or effortless selective undo.

verification.question: After offline editing, reopening, and version restoration, which exact copy and changes exist locally and remotely, and does the displayed status agree?

principles.title: Let people retrieve and refine by what they remember

source.heading: AF-16 — Let people retrieve and refine by what they remember

triggers: Search, catalogs, history, filters, or large collections.
principles.exceptions: Avoid unrestricted history retention or invisible query changes. The book's database limitations and natural-language pessimism are historical assertions, not current technical constraints. Search does not eliminate a useful browse structure.

verification.question: Can people retrieve an item with partial wording, refine constraints, recover from no results, and return without losing the query or place?

principles.title: Prevent predictable mistakes and provide honest reversibility

source.heading: AF-17 — Prevent predictable mistakes and provide honest reversibility

triggers: Destructive actions, exploration, adjustment, history, or a decision whose effect is hard to foresee.
principles.exceptions: Some effects cannot be undone. Selective history reversal can have dependencies. Do not suppress necessary consent or replace critical failure cues with silence; visual and audible feedback must have accessible equivalents.

verification.question: After intervening edits or navigation, does undo restore its stated scope, and are irreversible external effects still disclosed?

principles.title: Build inclusion, localization, and useful help into the flow

source.heading: AF-18 — Build inclusion, localization, and useful help into the flow

triggers: Any user-facing flow, particularly compact screens, time limits, customization, or unfamiliar features.
principles.exceptions: Do not default to a separate accessibility mode or assume accessibility personas are secondary. The book's contrast percentages, timing multiples, flash rates, and tour lengths are not current standards. Placeholder hints do not replace persistent labels.

verification.question: Can the task be completed with required assistive input, enlarged text, relevant locales, and interruptions, with remaining access limits recorded?

principles.title: Make hierarchy, grouping, and visual language express the task

source.heading: AF-19 — Make hierarchy, grouping, and visual language express the task

triggers: Screen composition, system tokens, charts, visual critique, or inconsistent screens.
principles.exceptions: Visual restraint must not erase discoverability or legibility. A fixed grid, golden ratio, font minimum, or muted palette is not a universal recipe. Correlation is not causation, despite the source's loose language; its numerical geometry typo is excluded.

verification.question: With realistic long and sparse content, do intended users associate the correct labels, values, and actions and identify the priority for their task?

principles.title: Keep task controls in context and define dialog commitment

source.heading: AF-20 — Keep task controls in context and define dialog commitment

triggers: Editors, secondary panes, sheets, dialogs, or repeated adjustment.
principles.exceptions: Modeless controls are not always preferable; space, focus, and consequences matter. Do not impose historical fullscreen, close-button, or OK/Cancel conventions on modern iOS or web.

verification.question: During repeated edits and changed selection, what survives back, cancel, dismiss, and commit, and does it match the displayed interaction contract?

principles.title: Make command scope, state, and activation unmistakable

source.heading: AF-21 — Make command scope, state, and activation unmistakable

triggers: Selection, bulk actions, toggles, active tools, or drag-and-drop.
principles.exceptions: Use contemporary platform behavior rather than hand-implementing historical drag thresholds or modifier keys. Common media conventions need not be replaced because the author prefers another representation.

verification.question: Can users identify the affected scope before activation, including offscreen selection, and cancel a drag or mode without unintended effects?

principles.title: Adapt mobile structure while preserving each destination's place

source.heading: AF-22 — Adapt mobile structure while preserving each destination's place

triggers: Native iOS navigation, phone/tablet variants, or an interrupted mobile task.
principles.exceptions: Mobile is not uniformly transient or subordinate to desktop. Old tab counts, placements, aspect ratios, drawer conventions, and integration limits require contemporary evidence. Do not retain sensitive state indiscriminately.

verification.question: When switching destinations, resizing where supported, and returning after interruption, are location, selection, and appropriate work preserved?

principles.title: Preserve orientation through scrolling, reflow, and return

source.heading: AF-23 — Preserve orientation through scrolling, reflow, and return

triggers: Responsive web pages, infinite collections, long documents, or content that changes size.
principles.exceptions: Infinite loading suits some browsing tasks and harms others. Not every page needs a sticky header, parallax, or an overview. The source's fixed breakpoint and historical browser assumptions are not specifications.

verification.question: After opening a deep item, returning, and relevant content-size or layout changes, can the person retain orientation and reach persistent actions? Include keyboard navigation on supported surfaces.

principles.title: Communicate progress and failure with a concrete recovery route

source.heading: AF-24 — Communicate progress and failure with a concrete recovery route

triggers: Loading, offline work, failed saving, notifications, or confirmation dialogs.
principles.exceptions: A spinner is not proof of server progress. Do not hide material failures, promise rollback that the backend cannot provide, or remove appropriate informed confirmation because the source argues against dialogs.

verification.question: Under failure and partial completion, does feedback accurately identify retained work, pending effects, and a safe retry or cancellation route?

principles.title: Define the person's outcome before the interface

source.heading: DI-01 — Define the person's outcome before the interface

triggers: Starting a screen, feature, or research brief.
principles.exceptions: Applies to iOS and web. An urgent small change can use a brief assumption record; do not invent research findings to fill it.

verification.question: Does the brief name the person's outcome, context, existing behavior, and unknowns, with a traceable basis for audience claims?

principles.title: Deliver useful value before asking for avoidable decisions

source.heading: DI-02 — Deliver useful value before asking for avoidable decisions

triggers: First use, onboarding, registration, setup, or a largely empty initial screen.
principles.exceptions: Deferral is inappropriate when a choice is necessary to protect the user's interests or correctly perform the task. The goal is useful progress, not pressure to commit.

verification.question: Starting with no account or data, can people reach a useful result before optional setup while understanding unavoidable decisions?

principles.title: Preserve context through interruption, exploration, and return

source.heading: DI-03 — Preserve context through interruption, exploration, and return

triggers: A multistep task, drilldown, switching views, backgrounding, or resuming work.
principles.exceptions: Persistence has security and data-freshness constraints; define expiration and recovery explicitly. Preserving a stale value silently is not always helpful.

verification.question: After a partly completed task is left and reopened, do the appropriate values, selection, filters, location, and status survive under the stated expiration policy?

principles.title: Support growing fluency without hiding the basic route

source.heading: DI-04 — Support growing fluency without hiding the basic route

triggers: Repeated data entry, frequent commands, or mixed novice and expert audiences.
principles.exceptions: Do not add macros or workspace customization to an occasional simple task merely because the pattern exists. On touch devices, shortcuts need discoverable alternatives.

verification.question: Does the basic route remain discoverable on first use, while the tenth repetition benefits from predictable shortcuts or batching with reviewable scope?

principles.title: Organize objects and tasks before choosing screen furniture

source.heading: DI-05 — Organize objects and tasks before choosing screen furniture

triggers: New information architecture, ambiguous navigation, or screens with unrelated content.
principles.exceptions: Exclusive categories are one organizing technique, not a mandate to eliminate legitimate facets or tags. An organization chart is not automatically the user's mental model.

verification.question: Can users classify realistic and awkward items and explain the roles of overview, detail, creation, and action screens without conflicting labels?

principles.title: Select patterns by preconditions and costs

source.heading: DI-06 — Select patterns by preconditions and costs

triggers: Choosing among a wizard, settings page, modal, dashboard, list, or custom composition.
principles.exceptions: Patterns can be combined or adapted. A novel arrangement needs a clear rationale and evaluation; it does not need to imitate a reference to be legitimate.

verification.question: Does the chosen pattern's rationale name the user problem, fitting conditions, introduced cost, and a plausible rejected alternative?

principles.title: Make location, destination, and return understandable

source.heading: DI-07 — Make location, destination, and return understandable

triggers: Global navigation, nested content, deep links, or neighboring-item browsing.
principles.exceptions: Not every screen needs every destination; focused tasks can reduce navigation. Web breadcrumbs and historical menu placements are not automatic iOS requirements.

verification.question: On direct entry and return, can a person identify the destination and use back, up, or next according to the actual history, hierarchy, or sequence?

principles.title: Guide a sequence without trapping the user

source.heading: DI-08 — Guide a sequence without trapping the user

triggers: Checkout, onboarding, permissions, application forms, or other dependent steps.
principles.exceptions: Do not split a simple task merely to create progress. Random-access configuration and repeated expert work may need another structure. A step indicator is different from a background-operation progress bar.

verification.question: Can users explain their current step, correct an earlier answer, exit with predictable retention, and reach a truthful completion state?

principles.title: Match collection presentation to the user's collection task

source.heading: DI-09 — Match collection presentation to the user's collection task

triggers: Search results, catalogs, feeds, libraries, or card grids.
principles.exceptions: A carousel suits exploratory browsing better than precise finding or simultaneous comparison. Infinite loading is not a universal replacement for bounded navigation. Split view needs usable space after content and accessibility adaptations.

verification.question: With empty, long, and changing collections, can people perform the actual browse, find, compare, or selection task and keep their place on return?

principles.title: Hide secondary detail only when the task can tolerate it

source.heading: DI-10 — Hide secondary detail only when the task can tolerate it

triggers: Tabs, accordions, collapsible panels, inlays, or dense forms.
principles.exceptions: Module tabs fit a small stable set whose contents need not be seen together. Multiple expanded sections may be appropriate; a single-open accordion is not a universal law.

verification.question: Can people view the information needed together for their decision, discover secondary detail, and retain context when it expands?

principles.title: Use hierarchy and spacing to communicate relationships

source.heading: DI-11 — Use hierarchy and spacing to communicate relationships

triggers: A screen feels cluttered, flat, disconnected, or difficult to scan.
principles.exceptions: Dense expert tools and spacious editorial experiences can both work. Reading order, text size, content, and task determine useful density.

verification.question: At the intended text size and with long labels, do visual groups preserve real relationships and help people identify the primary task content and action?

principles.title: Maintain a visual framework across the complete flow

source.heading: DI-12 — Maintain a visual framework across the complete flow

triggers: Combining references, extending an existing product, or designing multiple screen families.
principles.exceptions: Consistency allows variation. A media canvas, settings page, and purchase confirmation do not need identical layouts, and platform conventions can require distinct components.

verification.question: Across entry, work, success, and failure states, do repeated type roles, regions, and control treatments retain the same meaning?

principles.title: Give visual expression an intentional job

source.heading: DI-13 — Give visual expression an intentional job

triggers: Choosing a visual direction, imagery, texture, illustration, or degree of ornament.
principles.exceptions: Cultural associations and aesthetic preferences vary. Long-use work tools may need a quieter treatment than a short promotional experience. A beautiful reference does not demonstrate improved trust or conversion for this product.

verification.question: Do coherent alternatives express the intended feeling with representative content, and do audience responses support any claimed emotional effect?

principles.title: Make visual distinctions readable and semantically reliable

source.heading: DI-14 — Make visual distinctions readable and semantically reliable

triggers: Type selection, color roles, icons, status indicators, or visual polish.
principles.exceptions: The book's point-size suggestions and broad font/color associations are not current accessibility specifications. Verify platform requirements and contrast separately. Never reduce helper text to illegibility merely to make it visually secondary.

verification.question: In actual themes and text sizes, are names, numbers, icons, and states distinguishable through more than color, and can people interpret unfamiliar actions?

principles.title: Design mobile around context and capabilities

source.heading: DI-15 — Design mobile around context and capabilities

triggers: An iOS screen, an adaptive interface, or a web concept being translated to mobile.
principles.exceptions: Do not blindly remove needed functionality. The book contains obsolete device assumptions and dimensions; it cannot define today's iOS APIs, safe areas, text behavior, or target-size requirements. Its Bottom Navigation pattern is a mobile-web footer, not an iOS tab bar.

verification.question: In the intended mobile context, do touch, reentry, and justified device integrations reduce effort while keeping needed capabilities and understandable consent?

principles.title: Make actions discoverable and their scope explicit

source.heading: DI-16 — Make actions discoverable and their scope explicit

triggers: Toolbars, contextual actions, gestures, menus, or a crowded action area.
principles.exceptions: Contextual controls can reduce clutter for occasional expert actions. They should not make an essential route unavailable on another input method or obscure why an action is unavailable.

verification.question: Can people discover the essential action and its affected object using touch or keyboard, including understanding unavailable actions and their prerequisites?

principles.title: Make commitment and recovery part of the action model

source.heading: DI-17 — Make commitment and recovery part of the action model

triggers: Saving, submitting, deleting, purchasing, or performing a costly operation.
principles.exceptions: Not every action needs a confirmation or preview. Do not promise transactional reversibility the backend cannot provide. The book's examples of irreversible actions and undo-stack sizes are contextual, not universal policies.

verification.question: Where exactly does the action commit, and do preview, cancel, undo, and recovery perform only the guarantees shown before that point?

principles.title: Show honest progress while keeping useful work available

source.heading: DI-18 — Show honest progress while keeping useful work available

triggers: Loading, saving, search, upload, refresh, or other asynchronous work.
principles.exceptions: Background concurrency must not imply that stale or uncommitted data is final. Partial content is useful only when its incompleteness is clear. Avoid treating the book's timing examples as universal thresholds.

verification.question: Under slow, partial, failed, retried, and canceled work, does the indicator match real progress while usable content remains accurately marked?

principles.title: Design data displays around the question and comparison

source.heading: DI-19 — Design data displays around the question and comparison

triggers: A dashboard, report, chart, metric card, or analytical overview.
principles.exceptions: A shared time axis with stacked separate plots is different from an arbitrary overlaid dual-axis chart. Small multiples need enough room for their information to remain legible; not every desktop analysis transfers unchanged to a phone.

verification.question: Using the display's actual values and scales, can intended users answer its stated lookup, trend, outlier, or comparison question?

principles.title: Let people narrow data without losing orientation

source.heading: DI-20 — Let people narrow data without losing orientation

triggers: Search filters, datatips, linked charts, dynamic queries, or dense analytical content.
principles.exceptions: Hover-only details do not translate to touch. Multi-view brushing requires space and consistent entity identity. An empty filtered result needs a recovery path, not an unexplained blank canvas.

verification.question: Can users identify and reset active constraints, access detailed values by required input methods, and recover from an empty filtered result?

principles.title: Treat every form field as work to justify

source.heading: DI-21 — Treat every form field as work to justify

triggers: Registration, checkout, profile editing, settings, or information collection.
principles.exceptions: A placeholder is not a substitute for a persistent label. Top-aligned labels are an option, not a universal layout rule. A sentence-style input can clarify a relationship but may need restructuring in another language.

verification.question: Does every requested field serve the task, and can people interpret its persistent label and required status with the relevant locale and keyboard?

principles.title: Assist entry without overruling intent

source.heading: DI-22 — Assist entry without overruling intent

triggers: Formatting rules, autocomplete, default values, or complex selection controls.
principles.exceptions: Structured entry fits genuinely fixed formats; names, addresses, and international telephone numbers often are not fixed. Avoid defaults for sensitive assumptions or consequential consent. Suggestions must not interfere with ordinary typing.

verification.question: Do paste, unusual valid formats, and rejected suggestions preserve the person's intended value while making consequential defaults inspectable and changeable?

principles.title: Keep error correction beside the work

source.heading: DI-23 — Keep error correction beside the work

triggers: Validation, rejected submission, conflicting values, or an interrupted form.
principles.exceptions: Do not show an invalid-state message simply because someone has started typing a potentially valid value. Disabled submission is not a universal solution; users still need to understand unmet requirements. Password examples in this book are not current security requirements.

verification.question: After an actual failed submission, can people identify and correct the relevant field without losing other work or relying on color alone?

principles.title: Build a design system that preserves intent across platforms

source.heading: DI-24 — Build a design system that preserves intent across platforms

triggers: Implementing several screens, coordinating agents, or extending a component library.
principles.exceptions: Web framework examples are historical illustrations, not technology recommendations or native iOS specifications. Consistent identity need not mean identical widgets. A library should enable a justified experience rather than prohibit it.

verification.question: Can the shared system assemble complete flows with consistent meaning and specified states while supporting justified native platform variants?

principles.title: Design for the task the person expects to perform

source.heading: JJ-01 — Design for the task the person expects to perform

triggers: Navigation, a first-use screen, a changing interface, or a potentially ambiguous control.
principles.exceptions: Familiarity varies by audience. Consistency does not justify preserving an established error or misleading label. Repeated confirmations can become habitual rather than protective.

verification.question: What do first-time and returning users predict the recurring control will do, and which expectation conflicts with its actual meaning or changed state?

principles.title: Make visual groups match functional relationships

source.heading: JJ-02 — Make visual groups match functional relationships

triggers: Forms, grouped controls, lists, dashboards, or a screen with several competing regions.
principles.exceptions: No universal ban on borders or nested containers follows from Gestalt principles. Strong grouping can also hide meaningful differences.

verification.question: After wrapping and text enlargement, do spacing, alignment, and shared styling still group each label, value, and action with its intended relationship?

principles.title: Structure information around the comparison or decision

source.heading: JJ-03 — Structure information around the comparison or decision

triggers: Summaries, account details, results, prices, or long blocks of instructions.
principles.exceptions: Visual chunking is not a reason to fragment a text field or impose one culturally specific number/date format. Input flexibility and assistive reading order still matter.

verification.question: Can intended users answer the actual comparison question without misreading label-value associations or calculating a total the display could provide?

principles.title: Give important color meanings another perceivable cue

source.heading: JJ-04 — Give important color meanings another perceivable cue

triggers: Validation, status, selection, charts, or color-coded categories.
principles.exceptions: A grayscale or color-vision simulation is a diagnostic aid, not proof of accessibility. Avoid inferring universal cultural meanings or accessibility from color names.

verification.question: For each meaningful status, selection, or chart distinction, is equivalent information available beyond color in the implemented content and semantics?

principles.title: Put feedback where attention is likely to be

source.heading: JJ-05 — Put feedback where attention is likely to be

triggers: Form errors, success messages, warnings, asynchronous results, or a small change elsewhere on screen.
principles.exceptions: Do not prescribe blinking, shaking, sound, or a modal for every error. Repetition causes habituation; animation may distract or cause discomfort. Current platform semantics govern implementation.

verification.question: While attending to the triggering field or control, do intended users notice the resulting status and recovery route, including with required assistive feedback?

principles.title: Reduce reading work without removing meaning

source.heading: JJ-06 — Reduce reading work without removing meaning

triggers: Onboarding, help, error text, empty states, settings, or dense content.
principles.exceptions: Brevity does not justify ambiguous labels, cryptic icons, missing consequences, or inaccessible tiny text. Do not adopt the discredited whole-word-outline account of reading discussed in the book.

verification.question: With realistic enlarged and localized content, can intended users explain the essential instruction and consequence without missing meaning removed for brevity?

principles.title: Keep task state outside the user's memory

source.heading: JJ-07 — Keep task state outside the user's memory

triggers: Multi-step input, editing, search, modes, comparisons, or returning to a task.
principles.exceptions: There is no justified universal seven-item menu limit. Externalizing state must respect privacy and avoid overwhelming the screen with irrelevant detail. Historical password-hint/security-question examples are not current authentication advice.

verification.question: Which facts must people remember across screens, and after interruption can they recover task position and relevant prior input from the interface?

principles.title: Make interruption and resumption part of the flow

source.heading: JJ-08 — Make interruption and resumption part of the flow

triggers: Notifications, app switching, backgrounding, permission detours, multi-step work, or delayed completion.
principles.exceptions: These iOS scenarios are adaptations of the attention principle, not platform prescriptions from the book. Avoid excessive badges or repeated announcements that compete with the task.

verification.question: After backgrounding, a permission detour, or connectivity loss, is work preserved and can people identify what changed, what remains, and the next action?

principles.title: Make the next action's destination and consequence clear

source.heading: JJ-09 — Make the next action's destination and consequence clear

triggers: Navigation labels, menu items, destructive actions, or ambiguous dialogs.
principles.exceptions: A longer literal label is not automatically better; space, localization, familiarity, and accessibility must be assessed together. Novel symbols need a discoverable meaning.

verification.question: What destination or consequence do intended users predict from the label, and does activation affect that exact operation or scope?

principles.title: Optimize mental effort as well as action count

source.heading: JJ-10 — Optimize mental effort as well as action count

triggers: Choosing between a familiar multi-step flow and a compact novel interaction; expert shortcuts; redesigns.
principles.exceptions: Do not use a fixed tap budget, assume every shorter flow is better, or preserve complexity merely because experts learned it. Current iOS conventions constrain gesture design.

verification.question: Across first use and repeated use, which alternative reduces uncertainty, errors, and recovery effort rather than merely reducing the number of actions?

principles.title: Complete the whole job, including the ending

source.heading: JJ-11 — Complete the whole job, including the ending

triggers: Submission, checkout, saving, sharing, authentication, or leaving a task.
principles.exceptions: Automation must not silently commit consequential choices. Completion feedback must reflect the real system state.

verification.question: After the primary submission, are receipt, result retrieval, outstanding obligations, late failure, and safe exit consistent with the true terminal state?

principles.title: Prefer recognition where recall adds no value

source.heading: JJ-12 — Prefer recognition where recall adds no value

triggers: Commands, selection, history, settings, unfamiliar icons, or infrequent tasks.
principles.exceptions: A long option list can be harder than expressive search. Icons are not universally recognizable. Do not apply the book's historical visual-authentication examples as security designs.

verification.question: Where users must recall an exact command or item, can a relevant visible choice, example, history, or search reduce effort without creating an unmanageable list?

principles.title: Let the system calculate and explain what it knows

source.heading: JJ-13 — Let the system calculate and explain what it knows

triggers: Totals, eligibility, comparisons, configuration, constraints, and error diagnosis.
principles.exceptions: Expose assumptions and allow correction; a confident calculated answer based on hidden or stale data is worse than visible uncertainty. Do not treat simplified neuroscience in the explanatory chapters as a design requirement.

verification.question: Which required calculations or inferences can the product reliably supply, and are their assumptions, unavailable inputs, and correction paths visible?

principles.title: Establish a coherent conceptual model and vocabulary

source.heading: JJ-14 — Establish a coherent conceptual model and vocabulary

triggers: New product concepts, information architecture, overlapping features, or terminology drift.
principles.exceptions: A conceptual model is an explicit design hypothesis until supported by research. Internal implementation terminology and a familiar visual metaphor can both be poor fits.

verification.question: Can intended users explain where the task's objects live and what operations change them, using vocabulary consistent across navigation and feedback?

principles.title: Make safe exploration possible

source.heading: JJ-15 — Make safe exploration possible

triggers: First use, editing, experimentation, deletion, configuration, or unfamiliar controls.
principles.exceptions: An undo promise must actually restore the relevant state. Confirmation alone is weak protection against habitual action; not every reversible edit needs a dialog.

verification.question: After a plausible exploratory mistake, does the promised recovery restore the relevant work, and are irreversible effects explicit before action?

principles.title: Support informed decisions without exploiting framing

source.heading: JJ-16 — Support informed decisions without exploiting framing

triggers: Pricing, plans, defaults, permission requests, recommendations, and data presentation.
principles.exceptions: This skill's commitment to informed choice is an adaptation, not an endorsement of every persuasive example in the chapter. Do not encode a universal loss-aversion ratio, treat every person as irrational, or import old population statistics as current evidence.

verification.question: Can intended users compare accepting, declining, and changing a choice using the same material facts, without missing costs or consequences hidden by framing?

principles.title: Design the actual target and movement path

source.heading: JJ-17 — Design the actual target and movement path

triggers: Small controls, dense rows, drag gestures, sliders, menus, and one-handed interaction.
principles.exceptions: Desktop pointer-edge advantages do not transfer directly to touchscreens. Enlarging invisible targets must not create overlapping ambiguous hit regions.

verification.question: On the actual device and required input methods, can people acquire the real hit regions and complete or cancel precise movement without adjacent activation?

principles.title: Preserve responsiveness and honest progress

source.heading: JJ-18 — Preserve responsiveness and honest progress

triggers: Network requests, processing, transitions, long lists, loading, cancellation, or retry.
principles.exceptions: Historical timing ranges are context-sensitive approximations, not current universal budgets. Do not copy obsolete frame-rate targets, fake inert controls, fabricated progress, or cost-free-prefetch assumptions. Mobile energy, data, and privacy constrain speculative work.

verification.question: Under slow response, failure, retry, cancellation, and late success, does the flow acknowledge actions, preserve appropriate work, and avoid duplicate consequential effects?

principles.title: Scale effort to uncertainty and consequences

source.heading: UX-01 — Scale effort to uncertainty and consequences

triggers: Choosing research, modeling, prototype, or review depth.
principles.exceptions: A short deadline does not make unresolved high-impact behavior safe to assume.

verification.question: Which named uncertainty does each planned activity resolve, and where are unresolved high-impact questions and deferred checks recorded?

principles.title: Preserve the distinction between evidence and interpretation

source.heading: UX-02 — Preserve the distinction between evidence and interpretation

triggers: Turning observations, owner input, or competitor references into design claims.
principles.exceptions: A useful hypothesis need not await research; it must remain a hypothesis.

verification.question: Can a reader reconstruct a decision from observations, reports, constraints, precedents, and hypotheses without confusing their evidence types?

principles.title: Design for behavioral differences

source.heading: UX-03 — Design for behavioral differences

triggers: Selecting target users or resolving competing needs.
principles.exceptions: A primary target guides tradeoffs; it does not justify excluding other required users or access needs.

verification.question: For each audience attribute, is there evidence and a concrete changed decision concerning goals, expertise, context, or access?

principles.title: Model the journey outside the screen

source.heading: UX-04 — Model the journey outside the screen

triggers: Designing onboarding, transactions, cross-device work, or multi-party services.
principles.exceptions: A local component fix may need only the adjoining context, not a complete service map.

verification.question: Beyond the final screen, can people finish their real-world goal, and does every relevant external handoff have an owner and failure route?

principles.title: Specify capabilities and reasons before widgets

source.heading: UX-05 — Specify capabilities and reasons before widgets

triggers: Converting the brief or research into requirements.
principles.exceptions: An existing system or explicit request can legitimately constrain the widget.

verification.question: Does each requirement name a user capability and benefit, with acceptance behavior supported by actual save, sync, permission, or transaction guarantees?

principles.title: Establish a coherent conceptual model

source.heading: UX-06 — Establish a coherent conceptual model

triggers: New products, navigation overhauls, or repeated user confusion.
principles.exceptions: A decorative theme need not become a literal interaction metaphor.

verification.question: Can intended users predict what an action changes and explain where information lives without contradictory concepts or misleading metaphors?

principles.title: Treat information architecture as object structure

source.heading: UX-07 — Treat information architecture as object structure

triggers: Lists, detail views, search, filters, saved items, or shared content.
principles.exceptions: A small feature may inherit a suitable existing model.

verification.question: Can people reach the same object through different paths with consistent identity, terminology, state, and sufficient decision attributes?

principles.title: Preserve meaning across devices while exposing limits

source.heading: UX-08 — Preserve meaning across devices while exposing limits

triggers: iPhone/iPad/web variants, synchronization, account continuity, or constrained data.
principles.exceptions: Different device roles can justify different capabilities.

verification.question: When a task moves between devices, do identity and appropriate work survive, and can people distinguish absent data from unavailable or unsynced data?

principles.title: Explore alternatives without treating precedent as a cage

source.heading: UX-09 — Explore alternatives without treating precedent as a cage

triggers: New interaction concepts or a brief that prematurely specifies a solution.
principles.exceptions: Do not reopen settled constraints for novelty alone.

verification.question: Do alternatives address the same goal through meaningfully different structures or decision support, with explicit reasons for choosing and evaluating one?

principles.title: Make transitions a first-class design object

source.heading: UX-10 — Make transitions a first-class design object

triggers: Any screen sequence or consequential action.
principles.exceptions: Not every transition needs animation; feedback can be stable content or a state change.

verification.question: For each consequential transition, are prerequisites, intermediate states, feedback, next actions, and recovery defined, and can people recognize whether the goal advanced?

principles.title: Support interruption and re-entry

source.heading: UX-11 — Support interruption and re-entry

triggers: Long forms, authentication detours, permission prompts, error recovery, app switching, or multi-step decisions.
principles.exceptions: Privacy or shared-device constraints can require expiry or clearing; explain this and offer appropriate recovery.

verification.question: After a realistic authentication, permission, or error detour, can people resume with appropriate data and destination retained and pending work identifiable?

principles.title: Audit all five affordance roles

source.heading: UX-12 — Audit all five affordance roles

triggers: Reviewing a control, feedback message, or interaction mechanism.
principles.exceptions: Emotional appropriateness can mean quiet competence; every button does not need delight.

verification.question: For this task, does the control provide the needed function, communicate its meaning, remain perceivable and operable, and fit the intended emotional context?

principles.title: Make appearance and actual behavior agree

source.heading: UX-13 — Make appearance and actual behavior agree

triggers: Custom controls, cards, links, gestures, inactive actions, or action labels.
principles.exceptions: Established platform conventions can communicate some meaning implicitly; verify the intended audience recognizes them.

verification.question: Do the apparent target, implemented hit area, named consequence, selected scope, and prerequisites agree when users predict and activate the action?

principles.title: Optimize physical interaction for real conditions

source.heading: UX-14 — Optimize physical interaction for real conditions

triggers: Touch targets, maps, sliders, repeated actions, reach, and gesture-heavy iOS flows.
principles.exceptions: Bigger alone is not better when it creates accidental neighboring activation or obstructs content.

verification.question: Under relevant hand, device, and repeated-use conditions, can people hit or finely adjust the intended target without overshoot, occlusion, or neighboring activation?

principles.title: Distinguish visible, noticeable, readable, and distinguishable

source.heading: UX-15 — Distinguish visible, noticeable, readable, and distinguishable

triggers: Status, errors, actions, dense content, or subtle aesthetic treatments.
principles.exceptions: More visual salience everywhere destroys hierarchy.

verification.question: In relevant text-size, lighting, motion, and assistive conditions, can users notice feedback, read it, and distinguish states through dependable cues?

principles.title: Define emotional intent and express it coherently

source.heading: UX-16 — Define emotional intent and express it coherently

triggers: Visual direction, onboarding, trust-sensitive moments, repeated work, and product identity.
principles.exceptions: Avoid surprise or entertainment when it disrupts concentration or gravity. A mood board is direction, not proof of user response.

verification.question: Across major states, is the stated character expressed coherently, and what participant evidence supports any claim about trust or enduring attachment?

principles.title: Maintain a behavioral design system

source.heading: UX-17 — Maintain a behavioral design system

triggers: Reusable components or repeated implementation by multiple agents.
principles.exceptions: Platform differences and different task meanings can justify documented variants. Consistency supports prediction, but distinguishing dangerous actions or preserving context can matter more than identical appearance (ch32, pp810–814 / PDF839–843).

verification.question: Can builders implement applicable loading, empty, error, selection, disabled, and focus behavior from the shared component contract without inventing semantics?

principles.title: Choose prototype fidelity by the question

source.heading: UX-18 — Choose prototype fidelity by the question

triggers: Selecting what to sketch, mock, build, or test next.
principles.exceptions: High fidelity is useful when low fidelity would obscure the phenomenon under investigation.

verification.question: Does the prototype's breadth, depth, visual realism, and behavior suffice for the named question, with simulations and unsupported conclusions explicit?

principles.title: Keep prototypes honest enough to expose failure

source.heading: UX-19 — Keep prototypes honest enough to expose failure

triggers: Preparing a usability session or interactive review.
principles.exceptions: A deliberately narrow prototype is valid if its evaluation claims stay equally narrow.

verification.question: Do wrong turns, backtracking, corrections, and alternate valid routes behave plausibly without silent facilitator rescue, and are prototype limitations recorded?

principles.title: Name the evaluation and its evidence limits

source.heading: UX-20 — Name the evaluation and its evidence limits

triggers: A review report, subagent critique, or quality claim.
principles.exceptions: Inspection is valuable when participant access is unavailable; preserve its limitations.

verification.question: Does every conclusion identify the actual method and evidence, separating implementation observations, participant responses, and evaluator hypotheses?

principles.title: Connect goals to measures without false precision

source.heading: UX-21 — Connect goals to measures without false precision

triggers: Defining success, comparing alternatives, or reporting a UX score.
principles.exceptions: Numerical targets are optional when unsupported. Keep validated questionnaire wording and scoring intact unless explicitly reporting a modified instrument.

verification.question: Does each measure answer a stated user-goal question with an appropriate instrument and justified target, accounting for differences between comparison conditions?

principles.title: Test representative complete tasks

source.heading: UX-22 — Test representative complete tasks

triggers: Planning evaluation coverage.
principles.exceptions: A targeted study may isolate one issue, but cannot validate the whole flow.

verification.question: Does the evaluation cover representative frequent and critical tasks, meaningful alternatives, recovery, and required user types, with untested scope explicit?

principles.title: Avoid teaching the answer in the test

source.heading: UX-23 — Avoid teaching the answer in the test

triggers: Writing a task script or facilitating a session.
principles.exceptions: Collaborative co-design can use active discussion, clearly labeled as such.

verification.question: Can the participant task be understood without revealing interface labels or actions, and are assistance and prompting recorded separately from unassisted completion?

principles.title: Diagnose problems before prioritizing fixes

source.heading: UX-24 — Diagnose problems before prioritizing fixes

triggers: Synthesizing critique or participant observations into a backlog.
principles.exceptions: A speculative diagnosis may require another observation instead of immediate redesign.

verification.question: Does each finding preserve intent, expectation, observed outcome, consequence, uncertainty, and verification, with severity separated from cost and duplicate symptoms?

principles.title: Preserve coherence through delivery and retesting

source.heading: UX-25 — Preserve coherence through delivery and retesting

triggers: Implementation handoff, parallel agents, iteration, or release review.
principles.exceptions: Do not impose the book's exact sprint schedule, software tools, or complete-test repetition on every minor change.

verification.question: Does the running result preserve agreed behavior and visual intent, and does retesting the changed and relevant adjacent paths show the original blockage resolved without regression?

principles.title: Define scope, tasks, users, and risk before inspecting

source.heading: WI-01 — Define scope, tasks, users, and risk before inspecting

triggers: Starting research, design critique, implementation review, or release assessment.
principles.exceptions: Do not invent user research or choose only paths that flatter the design. A task script that reveals every control can hide discoverability problems.

verification.question: Does actual review coverage match the intended users, realistic task variants, frequent work, and rare consequential risks, with omissions recorded?

principles.title: Combine realistic task traversal with broader exploration

source.heading: WI-02 — Combine realistic task traversal with broader exploration

triggers: A review that currently examines isolated screenshots or only one scripted happy path.
principles.exceptions: Label capabilities unavailable in a static mockup as unverified. A screenshot cannot demonstrate input retention, latency, focus, or successful recovery.

verification.question: After priority task traversal, have plausible errors, alternate inputs, global components, and uncovered states been explored, with unavailable behavior marked unverified?

principles.title: Match inspection criteria to the product and make them testable

source.heading: WI-03 — Match inspection criteria to the product and make them testable

triggers: A generic checklist, vague quality claim, or imported design rule.
principles.exceptions: Do not turn contextual examples into universal restrictions, such as a fixed two-click limit. Exact platform and accessibility requirements require current authoritative verification.

verification.question: Can another reviewer apply the selected criterion to the same behavior and explain its relevance, observable result, and any uncertainty or inapplicability?

principles.title: Review independently before merging findings

source.heading: WI-04 — Review independently before merging findings

triggers: Multiple agents or people reviewing the same proposed flow or implementation.
principles.exceptions: Several agents sharing a model and source material are not independent human participants or a statistically independent sample. Repeated agreement is not validation. Do not equate a named agent role with domain credentials.

verification.question: Did reviewers record their own evidence and assumptions before seeing others' findings, and were disagreements resolved through evidence rather than vote counts?

principles.title: Use perspectives tied to goals and known constraints

source.heading: WI-05 — Use perspectives tied to goals and known constraints

triggers: Important risks are repeatedly missed, or a complex product serves different use patterns.
principles.exceptions: Do not simulate disability or demographics and claim lived-experience evidence. Age alone does not establish technology skill. The source itself notes limited guidance for choosing the most effective perspectives.

verification.question: Does each assigned perspective change concrete task questions or coverage, with unverified audience assumptions and evidence limits disclosed?

principles.title: Walk through every meaningful action and system response

source.heading: WI-06 — Walk through every meaningful action and system response

triggers: New or infrequent use, onboarding, a key transition, or an uncertain action label.
principles.exceptions: These are predictions about hypothetical users. A walkthrough does not establish actual completion rates, expert efficiency, or every valid alternative path. Choose action granularity appropriate to the task.

verification.question: For every meaningful step, what evidence supports the prediction that a new user would seek the subgoal, notice the action, connect it to the goal, and interpret the response?

principles.title: Keep expert inspection distinct from evidence from people

source.heading: WI-07 — Keep expert inspection distinct from evidence from people

triggers: Reporting a critique, agent walkthrough, automated check, or user session.
principles.exceptions: A multiagent review is not a pluralistic user study. A facilitated choice on a screenshot is not observed successful use of a working flow. If surrogates replace actual users, say so and limit conclusions.

verification.question: Do uses of tested, validated, users, and accessible accurately identify the method, artifact, people involved, conditions, and supported scope?

principles.title: Triangulate findings without treating repetition as proof

source.heading: WI-08 — Triangulate findings without treating repetition as proof

triggers: A speculative critique, disputed issue, incomplete access to users, or prioritization under uncertainty.
principles.exceptions: Several agents repeating one heuristic are one evidence lineage. Do not dismiss a severe observed failure because other methods missed it, or assume all reported complaints describe the same root cause.

verification.question: For a contested finding, which independent and current evidence supports or contradicts it, and is confidence kept separate from consequence?

principles.title: Write findings that can be reproduced and acted on

source.heading: WI-09 — Write findings that can be reproduced and acted on

triggers: Converting critique into a decision or implementation task.
principles.exceptions: Severity and confidence are separate judgments; neither is established by consensus alone. A typo can be critical if it changes meaning. Avoid inflated counts from duplicate instances or multiple descriptions of the same failure.

verification.question: Can someone unfamiliar with a finding reproduce or inspect its stated task and state, distinguish observation from preference, and tell what evidence would resolve it?

principles.title: Preserve strengths and examine tradeoffs when fixing

source.heading: WI-10 — Preserve strengths and examine tradeoffs when fixing

triggers: Redesigning after critique or resolving a conflict between principles.
principles.exceptions: Positive findings should identify behavior worth preserving, not merely soften criticism. A global redesign is not justified by one local problem without checking the broader pattern.

verification.question: After the correction, does the original failure resolve while adjacent successful tasks, audience needs, and useful behaviors remain supported?

principles.title: Track corrections through verification, not just recommendation

source.heading: WI-11 — Track corrections through verification, not just recommendation

triggers: A review produces issues, a designer proposes a fix, or an implementation claims completion.
principles.exceptions: Issue counts and a clean checklist are not proof of usability. Changes in counts can reflect reviewer coverage or reporting granularity rather than improved quality. Do not claim the book establishes a general ROI for formal usability inspections.

verification.question: Which accepted issues are implemented and verified against the original and adjacent conditions, and which remain deferred, disputed, or untested?

principles.title: Scale review formality to risk and maturity

source.heading: WI-12 — Scale review formality to risk and maturity

triggers: Choosing how much review to run for a small screen change, a new flow, or a consequential release.
principles.exceptions: Do not import the whole formal process, rigid staffing, or historical meeting times as mandatory agent ceremony. The book reports limited direct empirical validation of formal usability inspection effectiveness and ROI.

verification.question: Can the chosen review method answer the current risk question at this artifact's maturity, and is the next action clear where it cannot?

principles.title: Define the supported device context from the audience

source.heading: TD-01 — Define the supported device context from the audience

triggers: Selecting supported devices, browsers, inputs, or network conditions
A proposed mobile scope rests on the design team's preferred hardware
principles.exceptions: Scope support to actual audience needs and project commitments; historical market shares do not define current device coverage.

verification.question: Are compatibility decisions grounded in the audience and has the essential task run on representative supported devices?

principles.title: Check touch behavior on the actual hardware and in its environment

source.heading: TD-02 — Check touch behavior on the actual hardware and in its environment

triggers: Use with gloves, moisture, cases, styluses, or specialized touch hardware
Desktop simulation is being treated as proof of field touch performance
principles.exceptions: Test credible safe conditions and available equipment; avoid universal sensor assumptions or requiring users to compensate for poor sensing.

verification.question: Can users complete and recover from the task on the actual touch hardware under scoped operating conditions?

principles.title: Separate contact sensing, visible controls, and hand occlusion

source.heading: TD-03 — Separate contact sensing, visible controls, and hand occlusion

triggers: Choosing hit-region geometry, target spacing, or feedback placement
Finger breadth or sensor resolution is being used to justify universal target sizes
principles.exceptions: Contact geometry is not a universal accuracy model; honor current platform/accessibility requirements and assess actual selection and occlusion.

verification.question: Are hit regions, neighbors, feedback, and obscured content checked separately under plausible grips?

principles.title: Trace a design rule to its scope before translating it

source.heading: TD-04 — Trace a design rule to its scope before translating it

triggers: A borrowed numeric guideline conflicts with another requirement
Historical touch standards are being translated into a current interface
principles.exceptions: Criticism of an old rule cannot waive current binding requirements; verify source version, units, population, and device scope.

verification.question: Is the rule's scope and normative status recorded, with compliance and uncertain ergonomic claims checked separately?

principles.title: Preserve usability while grip, hand, and posture change

source.heading: TD-05 — Preserve usability while grip, hand, and posture change

triggers: A layout assumes one thumb zone or fixed handedness
A task changes between reaching, typing, scrolling, support positions, and return
principles.exceptions: Observed grip switching does not mean every person can safely switch; preserve task-required one-hand access and test actual constraints.

verification.question: Does the essential sequence remain usable through relevant grip and posture changes without avoidable reach, context loss, or accidental action?

principles.title: Keep observational findings attached to their sample and uncertainty

source.heading: TD-06 — Keep observational findings attached to their sample and uncertainty

triggers: Turning observational grip percentages into a product requirement
Using a null demographic result as proof that all groups have equivalent access
principles.exceptions: Convenience observation, country count, and absent significance do not establish representativeness or equivalence; preserve denominator and measurement limits.

verification.question: Are sample context, observation unit, denominator, exclusions, dates, and missing measures recorded before applying a reported finding?

principles.title: Keep essential actions available across input and orientation changes

source.heading: TD-07 — Keep essential actions available across input and orientation changes

triggers: Responsive or convertible interfaces permit touch, keyboard, pointer, or assistive input
Orientation or input changes while a task is unfinished
principles.exceptions: Scope input and orientation support explicitly; viewport or device classification cannot identify moment-to-moment grip or justify exclusive-input controls.

verification.question: Can supported input/orientation changes preserve task state, focus, essential actions, and usable content when the keyboard appears?

principles.title: Evaluate readability at the expected viewing distance

source.heading: TD-08 — Evaluate readability at the expected viewing distance

triggers: Scaling a phone layout to a tablet or supported display
Dense content must remain readable when the device is farther from the eyes
principles.exceptions: Device size is only an imperfect viewing-distance clue; preserve user text settings and avoid shrinking phone text or enforcing a universal scale.

verification.question: Can critical information be read and distinguished at plausible viewing distances and increased text sizes without unwanted zoom, leaning, or loss of function?

principles.title: Evaluate touch accuracy in its actual position and context

source.heading: TD-11 — Evaluate touch accuracy in its actual position and context

triggers: Small controls, densely packed navigation, frequent misses, or reusing one target geometry everywhere.
principles.exceptions: Do not replace current minimums with the book's smaller central targets or promote its 7–12 mm proposals and 95% contour into acceptance thresholds. A population aggregate does not establish every individual's precision, comfort, access needs, or grip. The author's kiosk caveat and later encumbrance findings limit transfer even when the hardware is an iPad. An inability or unwillingness to shift grip remains a valid requirement for a particular audience.

verification.question: Which actual target positions, neighboring actions, and use contexts were exercised, and what misses or unintended activations remain?

principles.title: Let people bring important content into a usable viewing position

source.heading: TD-12 — Let people bring important content into a usable viewing position

triggers: Long forms, the last list row or paragraph, a keyboard-covered action, or an interface that stops scrolling exactly at the viewport boundary.
principles.exceptions: Do not center every control, force all secondary controls to edges, impose a four-tab limit, or discard platform navigation conventions. A fixed control may be appropriate. Excessive padding and surprising automatic scrolling can themselves cost effort or disorient. The source critiques the F-pattern as a universal composition recipe; replacing it with another universal location rule would repeat that mistake.

verification.question: Can final content and actions be brought into a usable viewing position with the relevant keyboard, chrome, text size, and scroll behavior?

principles.title: Make action feedback visible despite finger occlusion

source.heading: TD-13 — Make action feedback visible despite finger occlusion

triggers: A small icon changes state under the finger, selection feels unresponsive, or input acknowledgement is hard to notice.
principles.exceptions: A bigger invisible hit region alone does not solve obscured feedback. A pressed appearance acknowledges input, not successful remote completion. Do not mandate flashing, haptics, sound, text labels on every familiar icon, or a large colored box around every action. Haptics can supplement but cannot replace accessible feedback, and current system/user preferences govern their use.

verification.question: While the control is touched and after release, is the activated object and its accepted, pending, or completed state perceivable despite finger occlusion?

principles.title: Support correction in precision touch tasks

source.heading: TD-14 — Support correction in precision touch tasks

triggers: Drawing, text placement, handles, fine sliders, cropping, dragging, or accidental drag activation during a tap.
principles.exceptions: Do not hard-code optical offsets, activate consequential actions on touch-down, or replace native gesture thresholds from the book's simplified mouse/touch event explanation. Display hardware, APIs, input device, and accessibility settings vary. Snapping must not silently overrule intended placement; precision aids need understandable exits.

verification.question: Can precise selections be inspected, corrected, and canceled without unintended drags or silent snapping that changes intent?

principles.title: Keep scrolling compatible with reading and selection

source.heading: TD-15 — Keep scrolling compatible with reading and selection

triggers: Dense lists/tables, a feed full of interactive rows, scrolling that accidentally activates content, or support for different writing directions.
principles.exceptions: Do not reserve a permanent empty column, force left alignment for every locale, or ban horizontal and two-axis interaction where the task requires them. The chapter's final “always left-aligned” checklist must be read with its explicit RTL discussion. Cards, charts, maps, and visual canvases need task-specific behavior rather than universal text-list treatment.

verification.question: Can people scroll and select the actual content without unintended activation or lost orientation, including relevant writing directions?

principles.title: Inspect the actual hit regions and their neighboring consequences

source.heading: TD-16 — Inspect the actual hit regions and their neighboring consequences

triggers: Icons that appear well separated, custom button markup, compact rows, nested actions, or a mismatch between a visible container and its tappable area.
principles.exceptions: A hand overlay or probability circle is an inspection aid, not measured task performance. Do not expand regions until they overlap, make every containing card a button, or consume scroll space with an unintended action. Separate actions inside a row require deliberate semantics. The book's specific probability radius/diameter language should not become an implementation formula.

verification.question: Do the actual hit regions match the intended control surfaces without ambiguous overlap, and what does a near miss activate?

principles.title: Design recovery around the consequence of a mistaken tap

source.heading: TD-17 — Design recovery around the consequence of a mistaken tap

triggers: Submit versus Cancel, Delete near frequent actions, accidental navigation, or a touch mistake that could lose work or commit an external action.
principles.exceptions: Do not remove Cancel, Clear, reset, or confirmation solely because the author disfavors them; these may express a real user intent or required protection. Do not hide every consequential command in a low-use menu or promise undo when an external effect cannot be reversed. Preserve necessary consent and distinguish a compensating action from true rollback.

verification.question: After a plausible mistaken tap, what has actually committed, which work survives, and can the user safely correct or recover?

principles.title: Treat environment and access conditions as part of the task

source.heading: TD-18 — Treat environment and access conditions as part of the task

triggers: A mobile task may occur with occupied hands, glare, noise, motion, divided attention, or different sensory/motor capabilities.
principles.exceptions: Temporary constraints are useful design prompts, not a replacement for disabled people's actual requirements or dedicated accessibility checks. Do not claim that designing for noise or glare makes an interface work for every user. Security/expiry may require timeouts; give understandable notice, preservation, extension, or recovery where appropriate. Do not turn every notice into a permanent obstruction.

verification.question: Which plausible environment, interruption, hand-availability, and access conditions have been checked, and which remain assumptions or unsupported?

principles.title: Make rapid repeated and unintended input safe across state changes

source.heading: TD-19 — Make rapid repeated and unintended input safe across state changes

triggers: A button can submit twice, toggle twice, open a confirmation under the same touch location, or start dragging when a tap was intended.
principles.exceptions: Do not disable all repeated input, suppress intended double-tap gestures, or introduce arbitrary delays into every control. Moving controls can disorient users or harm access; inspect the full interaction and native conventions. UI debouncing alone may not prevent duplicate server effects, while a confirmation alone may not prevent an accident.

verification.question: Do rapid repeated taps, delayed feedback, and state changes avoid duplicate or unintended committed actions without blocking intentional input?

principles.title: Verify edge controls with system chrome and real device constraints

source.heading: TD-20 — Verify edge controls with system chrome and real device constraints

triggers: Bottom actions, edge gestures, full-screen content, floating controls, browser chrome changes, or devices used with raised cases/bezels.
principles.exceptions: Do not ban bottom bars on the web or native apps, assume all edge gestures are unavailable, or add a universal 20% margin. Current supported devices, browser versions, system navigation modes, and cases differ. Visual padding alone does not prove correct hit testing or gesture handling.

verification.question: Do edge actions remain operable and content readable through actual keyboard, browser/system-chrome, orientation, and relevant case conditions?

principles.title: Give consequential meanings more than one dependable cue

source.heading: TD-21 — Give consequential meanings more than one dependable cue

triggers: Status icons, warnings, selection, charts, or controls distinguished mainly by color or a small symbol.
principles.exceptions: Shape meanings and prevalence claims are not universal; redundant cues need not add an icon to every label or replace meaningful platform semantics.

verification.question: Can each consequential state be identified without color alone, and can intended users explain an unfamiliar symbol's meaning?

principles.title: Make perceived interactivity and unavailable actions match reality

source.heading: TD-22 — Make perceived interactivity and unavailable actions match reality

triggers: Bordered status cards, minimalist inputs, selectable rows, ambiguous disabled controls, or an action that fails because a prerequisite is missing.
principles.exceptions: Bounding every action, hiding every unavailable feature, and disabling incomplete forms are author preferences; evaluate discovery, prerequisites, and current platform conventions.

verification.question: Do the perceived target, actual hit region, operation, and unavailable-state explanation agree when the person attempts the task?

principles.title: Check readable content in the actual viewing conditions

source.heading: TD-23 — Check readable content in the actual viewing conditions

triggers: Compact typography, long labels, small status graphics, large-screen variants, glare, or user-selected text enlargement.
principles.exceptions: Do not adopt historical physical-point tables, unit multipliers, upper size limits, or universal dark-mode claims; current platform guidance and actual viewing conditions govern checks.

verification.question: On representative devices and supported text settings, can people read critical labels and values without clipping or losing action access?

principles.title: Keep important feedback observable through touch and distraction

source.heading: TD-24 — Keep important feedback observable through touch and distraction

triggers: Selection feedback under a finger, transient notices, blinking status, actions used while moving, or adjacent consequential controls.
principles.exceptions: The source blink waveform and persist-until-dismissed rule are not universal. Recovery must reflect real reversibility; enlarged hit regions must not overlap neighboring controls.

verification.question: During realistic touch and interruption, can the person observe acknowledgement and recover from a mistap without unintended duplicate effects?

principles.title: Build reusable layouts from task priority and entry context

source.heading: TD-25 — Build reusable layouts from task priority and entry context

triggers: A product assembled from unrelated polished screens, an icon-grid landing page, competing task regions, or direct entry into deep content.
principles.exceptions: Center/edge/corner zones and fixed attribute rankings are contextual heuristics. Task priority, supported configurations, access needs, and current native conventions can justify other arrangements.

verification.question: On direct entry and after scrolling, can intended users identify the screen's role, current context, and main task without memorizing a route?

principles.title: Choose disclosure by context, comparison, and content length

source.heading: TD-26 — Choose disclosure by context, comparison, and content length
